title: Sweetness and humility
hook: mitthat neevee: sweetness and humility are the essence of all virtue (Asa di Var, ang 470)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukh, and your line: you are the Doer. Did something small that went wrong point you somewhere? Today Guru Nanak names two virtues he calls the essence of all the others. Day five hundred fifty-one.

An old shop scale hangs from a beam, two pans swinging under it. Put something in each pan and let go. One side rises, one side sinks. Which side is heavier? The side that goes down. It sounds too simple to matter. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak as a young storekeeper in Sultanpur, weighing out grain on scales like this one. In the Asa di Var, he turned the old market scale into a line Sikhs still quote today.
screen: `AN OLD SHOP SCALE.` → `WHICH SIDE IS HEAVIER?` → `THE SIDE THAT GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 470. At its center are two words: mitthat and neevee. Mitthat is sweetness, from mittha, sweet, the same word you'd use for sugar or a ripe mango. Neevee is lowliness, humility, being low. Mitthat neevee Nanakaa, the line goes: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtues and goodness. Not one virtue among many. The essence. Then the salok gives the scale. Everyone bows to themselves, it says, in paraphrase; no one bows to another. But put things on the balance and weigh them: the side that bends low is the heavy one. In the market, heavy means valuable. So the one who bows, who stays low, is the one with real weight. Why sweetness and humility together? Think of what each does without the other. Sweetness without humility can be charm: nice words that are really about being liked. Humility without sweetness can turn sour: a person so busy feeling small that they're cold to everyone. Together, they make someone easy to be near, who doesn't need to be above you and doesn't need to hurt you. The same salok opens with a tree and ends with a warning that bowing can be faked; we'll take both tomorrow. Some Sikhs sum up the whole path with these two words: sweet in speech, low in self. Two words, and a whole day of chances to practice them.
screen: `MITTHAT: SWEETNESS.` · `NEEVEE: HUMILITY.` · `THE SIDE THAT BENDS IS HEAVY.` · `SWEET IN SPEECH, LOW IN SELF.` · then, large: `THE ESSENCE OF ALL VIRTUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak sweetly once. Sit and think of one person you'll talk to today, especially one you tend to be short with. Picture the conversation. Find one sentence you could say more sweetly: softer, kinder, without the edge. Say it in your head a few times until it feels natural. Then picture yourself lower, not smaller, just unhurried and unguarded, like the heavy side of the scale. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Mitthat neevee, sweetness and lowliness: in Guru Nanak's salok, the essence of all virtue. On the scale, the side that bends low is the heavy one.
Your line: sweet and humble. Today, say your sweeter sentence to the person you pictured, and let them be right about one small thing. Day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs quote mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, as a summary of Sikh character, and hear it in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sweetness and lowliness; mittha means sweet, neeva means low.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice and modest.
what it means: sweetness and humility together are the essence of every virtue; the one who bends low has real weight.
what a scholar hears: the salok borrows the market balance, which tradition ties to Guru Nanak's years as a storekeeper, and makes the bending side the heavy one.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (simmal rukh saraaiaa ... mithat neevee Nanakaa), Ang 470

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm 'mithat neevee Nanakaa gun changiaaeeaa tat', 'sabh ko nivai aap kau par kau nivai na koe', the balance image ('dhar taaraajoo toleeai nivai so gauraa hoe') and 'sees nivaaiai kiaa theeai jaa ridai kusudhe jaahi'.
Transliteration in the index is 'mitthat'; Gurmukhi given as ਮਿਠਤੁ; confirm spelling.

Guru Nanak as a storekeeper (modikhana) in Sultanpur: from the janamsakhi tradition; linking the scale image to that work is the narrator's suggestion ('the kind he would have used'); confirm or soften.
The silk-cotton tree opens this same salok; it is held for day 552.
